title: Deconstruction of Buildings Law (Portland City Code Ch. 17.106)
summary: Requires full deconstruction (not mechanical demolition) of houses and duplexes built in 1940 or earlier, or designated historic, when seeking a demolition permit; salvaged materials may be sold, donated, or reused on site. Adopted 2016 with a 1916 cutoff; amended November 2019 to 1940, effective January 20, 2020.

title: San Antonio Deconstruction Ordinance
summary: Requires certain projects seeking a demolition permit to be deconstructed by a certified contractor rather than mechanically demolished, with pre- and post-deconstruction forms filed with the Office of Historic Preservation. Adopted September 8, 2022, effective October 1, 2022, in phases: initially structures built before 1920 and those in historic overlays; later phases extend to residential and accessory structures built in or before 1945 citywide, with older-structure thresholds in protected areas.

title: Deconstruction & Construction Materials Management Ordinance (PAMC 5.24)
summary: Ends demolition for whole-structure removals, residential and commercial: projects must complete a salvage survey designating materials for reuse, deconstruct the structure, and source-separate materials into separate containers. Effective July 1, 2020; local C&D diversion requirement is 80%, above the CALGreen 65% baseline. Builds on Palo Alto's 2015 residential deconstruction-survey requirement.

title: Sustainable Deconstruction Requirements (Ordinance 8366)
summary: All full structure removals and major remodels (Level 4 alterations), residential and commercial and regardless of building age, must file a sustainable deconstruction plan: at least 75% of the project's materials by weight reused, donated, or recycled, with a minimum of three structural material types diverted from landfill. Applies via the city's 2020 Energy Conservation Code and Ordinance 8366.

title: Executive Order: Building Deconstruction Policy
summary: Mayoral executive order (not a council ordinance) creating a building deconstruction policy: pilots deconstruction of condemned city-owned properties and city facilities, directs recovery and recycling standards for city-funded demolitions, and creates a Deconstruction Action Council to study expansion.

title: Construction and Demolition Debris Recovery Ordinance (Environment Code Ch. 14)
summary: Prohibits mixing construction and demolition debris with municipal solid waste and requires it to go to registered transporters and registered processing facilities for recovery, tied to building permits (Building Code 1302B for loads of one cubic yard or more). Jointly enforced by Building Inspection, Public Health, and the Environment Department. Updated by Ordinance 144-21, effective January 1, 2022, with new recovery requirements for transporters, facilities, and projects.

title: Construction & Demolition Disposal Bans and Salvage Assessment (SMC 21.36.089)
summary: Bans disposal of asphalt paving, bricks, and concrete in garbage at construction sites, later extended to metal, cardboard, gypsum scrap, and clean wood. Demolitions and alterations over 750 sq ft or $75,000 need a salvage assessment documenting reusable materials before work starts; whole-building demolitions need an approved salvage verifier.

title: Universal Recycling and Composting Ordinance (Waste No More) — construction & demolition requirements
summary: Voter-approved 2022 initiative (Waste No More), updated by City Council on September 15, 2025 as the Universal Recycling and Composting Ordinance. Construction and demolition projects over 500 sq ft, and interior remodels over 2,500 sq ft, must file a waste management plan before a permit issues and reuse or recycle at least 50% of debris across at least three material types. C&D documentation required from September 1, 2026.

title: Construction and Demolition Recycling Ordinance (City Code Ch. 15-6)
summary: General contractors on building permits over 5,000 sq ft of new, added, or remodeled floor area, and on commercial and multifamily demolitions of any size (from October 1, 2019), must divert at least 50% of project debris from landfill or dispose of less than 2.5 lb per sq ft, documented in a recycling report. Waivers require evidence of good-faith effort.

title: Construction or Demolition Site Waste Recycling (MCC 11-4-1905)
summary: Requires contractors on permitted construction and demolition (wrecking) projects to recycle or reuse a share of site debris: 25% for projects permitted from March 1, 2006, rising to 50% from January 1, 2007, reported on a C&D Debris Recycling Compliance Form. Debris contaminated with lead, asbestos, or other hazardous materials is excluded.

title: Single Use Foodware and Litter Reduction Ordinance (BMC Ch. 11.64)
summary: Requires reusable foodware for dining on the premises and charges customers for disposable cups (with an exemption for people with significant disabilities), to cut the street litter, marine pollution, and emissions caused by single-use disposable foodware and packaging.

title: Single-Use Food Ware Plastics, Toxics, and Litter Reduction Ordinance (Environment Code Ch. 16)
summary: Amends Environment Code Chapter 16 to prohibit single-use food service ware made with fluorinated chemicals (applied to compostable items from 2020) and certain plastic items, and to limit single-use plastic straws and accessories to customers who request them. Chapter 16 dates to 2006 (Ord. 295-06), which restricted polystyrene foam and required compostable or recyclable foodware.

title: Expanded Polystyrene Foam Ban (Local Law 142 of 2013)
summary: Bans the sale or offer of single-use expanded polystyrene foam food service items (cups, plates, trays, clamshells) and loose-fill packing peanuts, triggered by the Sanitation Commissioner's finding that EPS cannot be recycled in an environmentally effective, economically feasible way. Delayed by litigation; the ban took effect January 1, 2019.

title: Disposable Foodware Accessories Upon Request Ordinance
summary: Food and beverage facilities, including online ordering and third-party delivery platforms, may provide disposable accessories (utensils, condiments, straws, stirrers, napkins, lids, sleeves, trays) only when a customer requests them. Phased in by business size; builds on Ordinance 187028 (2019).

title: Food Service Ware Requirements (SMC 21.36.084 / 21.36.086)
summary: Banned expanded polystyrene food service ware from January 1, 2009, and required food service businesses to switch to compostable or recyclable single-use ware and packaging by July 1, 2010. Seattle Public Utilities issues temporary exceptions by Director's Rule SW-500.

title: Chicago Checkout Bag Tax (MCC Ch. 3-50)
summary: Tax on each paper or plastic checkout bag sold or used in the city: $0.07 from February 1, 2017, raised to $0.10 on January 1, 2025. Exempts bags for SNAP purchases and restaurant food or drink. Replaced the city's earlier plastic bag ban.

title: Single-Use Plastic Bag Ban (Bill 190610)
summary: Bans retailers from providing single-use plastic bags (including blown-film PLA bags) and paper bags with less than 40% recycled content. Effective July 1, 2021, with warnings only until full enforcement on April 1, 2022; minimum penalty $150.

title: Reduction of Checkout Bags by Retail Establishments (CBC 17-19)
summary: Bans thin plastic checkout bags and requires retailers to charge at least $0.05 for each recyclable paper, compostable, or reusable checkout bag, shown on the receipt; retailers keep the charge. Phased by store size from December 2018 through July 1, 2019.

title: Disposable Bag Fee
summary: Retailers must charge $0.10 per disposable bag (plastic, paper, or compostable) at checkout; the store keeps $0.04 and the city $0.06. Passed December 2019; start delayed by the pandemic to July 1, 2021.
